claim: The limit of detection (LOD) for COX-1 qPCR was determined at 20 sporozoites per sample with 8/8 sample positivity.
source: the limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) for COX-1 qPCR were determined at 20 sporozoites per sample (8/8 sample positivity with a coefficient of variation <2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A with serial dilutions of sporozoites assessed in octuplicate.

claim: The limit of quantification (LOQ) for COX-1 qPCR was determined at 20 sporozoites per sample with a coefficient of variation <2.
source: the limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ) for COX-1 qPCR were determined at 20 sporozoites per sample (8/8 sample positivity with a coefficient of variation <2) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating coefficient of variation measurements.

claim: COX-1 qPCR outperformed 18S rRNA gene target in detecting sporozoites.
source: COX-1 outperformed 18S in detecting sporozoites (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by comparative experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Integra dermal substitute artificial skin matrix had no apparent impact on sporozoite detectability and quantification.
source: The matrix had no apparent impact on sporozoite detectability and quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing sporozoite detection in different matrices shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mosquito infection prevalence was strongly associated with oocyst intensity, with a 14.68 times higher odds of infection prevalence associated with a tenfold higher oocyst density.
source: Mosquito infection prevalence was strongly associated with oocyst intensity, corroborating earlier work (Churcher et al., 2012), with a strong positive sigmoidal association and a 14.68 (95% CI, 8.18–26.35, p<0.0001) times higher odds of infection prevalence associated with a tenfold higher oocyst density.
evidence: Supported by logistic regression analysis of 457 mosquitoes and cited previous work by Churcher et al., 2012.

claim: There was no statistically significant difference in oocyst densities determined by day 8 mercurochrome staining (median five oocysts, IQR 2–20) and day 18 immunolabeling (median six oocysts, IQR 2–14).
source: We observed no statistically significant difference in oocyst densities determined by day 8 mercurochrome staining (median five oocysts, interquartile range [IQR], 2–20, N = 252) and day 18 immunolabeling (median six oocysts, IQR, 2–14, N = 167; Student's t-test on log densities, p=0.944).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison (Student's t-test) of experimental data from 406 mosquitoes.

claim: On day 9 post infection, 54.3% of highly infected mosquitoes (>50,000 sporozoites) were salivary gland sporozoite positive.
source: On day 9 PI, 54.3% of highly infected mosquitoes (>50,000 sporozoites) were salivary glands sporozoite positive (Figure 2A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Highly infected mosquitoes (>50,000 sporozoites) on day 9 PI had 3.17 times the odds of being salivary gland positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes (<1000 sporozoites), though this was not statistically significant.
source: On day 9 PI, 54.3% of highly infected mosquitoes (>50,000 sporozoites) were salivary glands sporozoite positive (Figure 2A) and had 3.17 (95% CI 95%, 0.7–14.4, p=0.4278) times the odds of being salivary gland positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes with <1000 sporozoites (27.3% salivary gland sporozoite positive).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with confidence intervals and p-value indicating lack of statistical significance.

claim: By day 10 PI, 82.2% of mosquitoes with 10,000–50,000 sporozoites were salivary gland positive and had 11.56 times the odds of being salivary gland positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes (<1000 sporozoites).
source: By day 10 PI, 82.2% of mosquitoes with 10,000–50,000 (10k–50k) sporozoites were salivary glands positive and had 11.56 (95% CI, 1.83, 73.25, p=0.0449) times the odds of being salivary glands positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes with <1000 sporozoites (28.6% salivary glands sporozoite positive).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with confidence intervals and p-value showing statistical significance.

claim: On day 11 PI, all 15 highly infected mosquitoes (>50,000 sporozoites) were salivary gland sporozoite positive.
source: On day 11 PI, all 15 highly infected mosquitoes (>50,000 sporozoites) were salivary glands sporozoite positive and meaningful odds ratios and 95% CIs could not be determined.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 15 mosquitoes.

claim: Over the entire EIP experiment period, mosquitoes with >50,000 sporozoites had a 13.44 times higher odds of being salivary gland positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes (<1000 sporozoites).
source: When considering the entire period over which EIP experiments were conducted, mosquitoes with >50,000 sporozoites had a 13.44 times higher odds of being salivary glands positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes (<1000 sporozoites; 95% CI, 4.02–44.88, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with confidence intervals and p-value showing strong statistical significance.

claim: Mosquitoes harboring 10,000–50,000 sporozoites had a 5.98 times higher odds of being salivary gland positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes (<1000 sporozoites).
source: Mosquitoes harboring 10,000–50,000 sporozoites had a 5.98 times higher odds of being salivary glands positive compared to low-infected mosquitoes (95% CI, 1.88–19.07, p=0.0119).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with confidence intervals and p-value showing statistical significance.

claim: EIP is shorter in high-infected compared to low-infected mosquitoes in a temperature- and humidity-controlled environment.
source: These data demonstrate that EIP is shorter in high-infected compared to low-infected mosquitoes in a temperature- and humidity-controlled environment.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing higher odds of salivary gland positivity at earlier time points for highly infected mosquitoes.

claim: The median sporozoite density per oocyst was 10,485 (IQR 9171.3–12,322.5) on day 9 post infection.
source: The median sporozoite density was 10,485 (IQR, 9171.3–12,322.5; 12 examined mosquitoes) per oocyst for day 9
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 12 mosquitoes with individual oocyst isolation and quantification.

claim: The median sporozoite density per oocyst was 15,390 (IQR 10,600–20,887) on day 10 post infection.
source: The median sporozoite density was 10,485 (IQR, 9171.3–12,322.5; 12 examined mosquitoes) per oocyst for day 9 and 15,390 (IQR, 10,600–20,887, 19 examined mosquitoes) for day 10 (Figure 2B, p=0.04995, by Welch's two-sample t-test on log10-transformed data).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 19 mosquitoes with statistical comparison showing significant difference.

claim: Sporozoite densities per oocyst increase significantly from day 9 to day 10 post infection (p=0.04995).
source: The median sporozoite density was 10,485 (IQR, 9171.3–12,322.5; 12 examined mosquitoes) per oocyst for day 9 and 15,390 (IQR, 10,600–20,887, 19 examined mosquitoes) for day 10 (Figure 2B, p=0.04995, by Welch's two-sample t-test on log10-transformed data).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (Welch's t-test) of experimental data.

claim: 5% (93/1854) of all oocysts were visually intact on day 18 post infection.
source: It was noted that a minority of oocysts failed to rupture during this time span; 5% (93/1854) of all oocysts were visually intact
evidence: Supported by microscopic examination data from 1854 oocysts.

claim: 88.3% (166/188) of examined mosquitoes had at least one unruptured oocyst on day 18 post infection.
source: 88.3% (166/188) of examined mosquitoes had at least one unruptured oocyst on day 18.
evidence: Supported by microscopic examination data from 188 mosquitoes.

claim: In 54% (12/22) of mosquitoes without evidence of ruptured oocysts, salivary gland sporozoites were observed.
source: In 54% (12/22) of mosquitoes without evidence of ruptured oocysts, we observed salivary gland sporozoites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 22 mosquitoes.

claim: There was a strong positive association between ruptured oocysts and salivary gland sporozoite load (ρ = 0.80, p<0.0001).
source: Nevertheless, there was a strong positive association observed between ruptured oocysts and salivary gland sporozoite load (ρ = 0.80, p<0.0001; N = 185) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis of experimental data from 185 mosquitoes.

claim: When intact oocysts were included in the analysis, the association between oocysts and salivary gland sporozoite load was nearly identical (ρ = 0.80, p<0.0001).
source: When intact oocysts were also included, this association was nearly identical (ρ = 0.80, p<0.0001; N = 185).
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis of experimental data from 185 mosquitoes.

claim: The median number of salivary gland sporozoites per ruptured oocyst in Anopheles stephensi was 4951 (IQR 3016–8318).
source: We estimated a median of 4951 (IQR, 3016–8318) salivary gland sporozoites per ruptured oocyst in Anopheles stephensi.
evidence: Estimated from experimental data analyzing the relationship between ruptured oocysts and salivary gland sporozoites.

claim: No qPCR signal was detected in the unexposed part of artificial skin in migration assessment experiments.
source: In three experiments with either 5 (N = 2) or 20 mosquitoes (N = 1) probing and feeding on the artificial skin, we detected a total of 3264, 3599, and 10,340 expelled sporozoites in the exposed skin part, respectively, but no qPCR signal in the unexposed part of artificial skin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from three experiments testing sporozoite migration.

claim: The sporozoite expelling procedure reliably captures all expelled sporozoites with no or negligible migration to the outer sides of the skin.
source: This indicates no or negligible migration of sporozoites to the outer sides of the skin and affirms that our procedure reliably captures all expelled sporozoites.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no qPCR signal in unexposed skin areas.

claim: 53% (116/216) of all mosquitoes used in skin feeding experiments expelled sporozoites at any density.
source: Among all mosquitoes used in skin feeding experiments, 53% (116/216) expelled sporozoites at any density
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 216 mosquitoes in artificial skin feeding experiments.

claim: 45% (97/216) of mosquitoes expelled sporozoites above the threshold for reliable detection and quantification of 20 sporozoites/skin.
source: Among all mosquitoes used in skin feeding experiments, 53% (116/216) expelled sporozoites at any density, and 45% (97/216) expelled sporozoites above our threshold for reliable detection and quantification of 20 sporozoites/skin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 216 mosquitoes with qPCR quantification.

claim: 33% (5/15) of mosquitoes that probed but failed to take a bloodmeal expelled sporozoites (sporozoite range 5–1802).
source: In line with previous work with rodent malaria species Plasmodium berghei (Matsuoka et al., 2002), sporozoite expelling was observed in mosquitoes that did not take a bloodmeal; 33% (5/15) of mosquitoes that probed but failed to take a bloodmeal expelled sporozoites (sporozoite range 5–1802).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 15 mosquitoes and cited previous work with P. berghei by Matsuoka et al., 2002.

claim: The correlation between oocyst sheets and total salivary gland sporozoite load remained highly similar and statistically significant when examining different ranges of oocyst intensity (<5, <10, <20 oocysts).
source: When examining this association for different ranges of oocyst intensity (<5, <10, <20 oocysts), correlation estimates remained highly similar and statistical significance was retained (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by stratified correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no statistically significant association between salivary gland infection intensity and the prevalence of expelling sporozoites (p=0.1880).
source: We observed no statistically significant association between salivary gland infection intensity and the prevalence of expelling sporozoites (Figure 3A; 95% CI, 0.74–0.85; p=0.1880).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data with confidence intervals and p-value.

claim: Among mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites, the median number of expelled sporozoites was 136 (IQR 34–501).
source: Among mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites, the medians of expelled and residual salivary gland sporozoites were 136 (IQR, 34–501) and 23,947 (IQR, 9127–78,380), respectively
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites.

claim: Among mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites, the median number of residual salivary gland sporozoites was 23,947 (IQR 9127–78,380).
source: Among mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites, the medians of expelled and residual salivary gland sporozoites were 136 (IQR, 34–501) and 23,947 (IQR, 9127–78,380), respectively
evidence: Supported by experimental data from mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites.

claim: The highest number of sporozoites detected in artificial skin was 4166.
source: Among mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites, the medians of expelled and residual salivary gland sporozoites were 136 (IQR, 34–501) and 23,947 (IQR, 9127–78,380), respectively, while the highest number of sporozoites detected in skin was 4166.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from artificial skin feeding experiments.

claim: There was a weak but statistically significant positive association between total sporozoite load and the number of expelled sporozoites (ρ = 0.35, p=0.0002) in An. stephensi mosquitoes.
source: We observed a weak but statistically significant positive association between total sporozoite load and the number of expelled sporozoites (ρ = 0.35, 95% CI, 0.17–0.50; p=0.0002; N = 112; Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis of experimental data from 112 mosquitoes.

claim: The correlation between total sporozoite load and expelled sporozoites remained highly similar when examining different ranges of total sporozoite load (<10,000; <50,000; <100,000 sporozoites), though lost statistical significance for loads <10,000 sporozoites (ρ = 0.29, p=0.1094).
source: When examining this association for different ranges of total sporozoite load (<10,000; <50,000; <100,000 sporozoites), correlation estimates remained highly similar although this correlation lost statistical significance when only including low total sporozoite loads <10,000 sporozoites (ρ = 0.29; 95% CI, –0.07 to 0.58, p=0.1094) (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by stratified correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: When including mosquitoes that did not expel any sporozoites, there was no statistically significant association between total sporozoite load and the number of expelled sporozoites (ρ = 0.016, p=0.8321).
source: When we included 26 observations from mosquitoes that did not expel any sporozoites, we observed no statistically significant association between total sporozoite load and the number of expelled sporozoites (ρ = 0.016, 95% CI, –0.12 to 0.16; p=0.8321).
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis including non-expelling mosquitoes.

claim: There was no evidence for a sharp increase in sporozoite expelling at sporozoite densities ≥10,000, as was previously described in rodent malaria models.
source: We observed no evidence for a sharp increase in sporozoite expelling at sporozoite densities ≥10,000, as was previously described in rodent malaria models Aleshnick et al., 2020
evidence: Based on analysis of experimental data and comparison with cited previous work by Aleshnick et al., 2020.

claim: 28% (53/186) of mosquitoes harbored sporozoites below 10,000 density.
source: We observed no evidence for a sharp increase in sporozoite expelling at sporozoite densities ≥10,000, as was previously described in rodent malaria models Aleshnick et al., 2020; 28% (53/186) of our mosquitoes harbored sporozoites below this density.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 186 mosquitoes.

claim: Among low-infected mosquitoes (<10,000 sporozoites), 64% (34/53) expelled sporozoites.
source: Among these low-infected mosquitoes, 64% (34/53) expelled sporozoites
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 53 low-infected mosquitoes.

claim: The median number of expelled sporozoites from low-infected mosquitoes (<10,000 total sporozoites) was 67 (IQR 13–128).
source: Among these low-infected mosquitoes, 64% (34/53) expelled sporozoites and the median number of expelled sporozoites was 67 (IQR, 13–128).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from low-infected mosquitoes that expelled sporozoites.

claim: Seven gametocyte donors (age 5–15 y; median 48 gametocytes/µl [range 40–167]) were recruited in Balonghin, Burkina Faso.
source: Seven gametocyte donors (age 5–15 y; median 48 gametocytes/µl [range 40–167]) were recruited in Balonghin, Burkina Faso.
evidence: Supported by recruitment data from field study in Burkina Faso.

claim: Five donors infected mosquitoes in at least one of the two feeding conditions (direct feeding or MACS enrichment).
source: Five donors infected mosquitoes in at least one of these two conditions (Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Mosquito infection rates and oocyst densities were significantly increased after gametocyte enrichment by MACS.
source: as expected, mosquito infection rates and oocyst densities were significantly increased after gametocyte enrichment.
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental data between direct feeding and MACS enrichment conditions.

claim: From a total of 53 mosquitoes in Burkina Faso experiments, salivary gland sporozoites were detected in 69% (37/53).
source: From a total of 53 mosquitoes, salivary gland sporozoites were detected in 69% (37/53).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 53 mosquitoes in Burkina Faso.

claim: 67.7% (23/31) of mosquito midguts had oocyst sheets detected by immunolabeling on day 19 in Burkina Faso experiments.
source: Also, 31 mosquito midguts were available for immunolabeling, of which 67.7% (23/31) had oocyst sheets detected by immunolabeling on day 19
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from 31 mosquito midguts.

claim: 48% (15/31) of mosquito midguts in Burkina Faso experiments had <5 oocyst sheets.
source: Also, 31 mosquito midguts were available for immunolabeling, of which 67.7% (23/31) had oocyst sheets detected by immunolabeling on day 19 and nearly half of these (48% [15/31]) had <5 oocyst sheets.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data from 31 mosquito midguts.

claim: Two mosquito midguts in Burkina Faso were negative by immunolabeling while their residual salivary gland sporozoite loads were 7958 and 14,750 respectively.
source: Two mosquito midguts were negative by immunolabeling while their residual salivary gland sporozoite loads were 7958 and 14,750 respectively, suggesting oocyst staining failure or rupture followed by complete oocyst disappearance.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from two mosquitoes with discordant results.

claim: 87.8% (370/421) of all detected oocysts ruptured in Burkina Faso experiments.
source: 87.8% (370/421) of all detected oocysts ruptured
evidence: Supported by microscopic examination data from 421 oocysts.

claim: 39% (9/23) of oocyst positive mosquitoes in Burkina Faso harbored at least one intact oocyst (range 1–19).
source: 87.8% (370/421) of all detected oocysts ruptured while 39% (9/23) of oocyst positive mosquitoes harbored at least one intact oocyst (range 1–19).
evidence: Supported by microscopic examination data from 23 oocyst-positive mosquitoes.

claim: Failure to rupture was uncommon in low-infected mosquitoes (≤5 oocysts, N = 80) where only two midguts had one intact oocyst.
source: Failure to rupture was uncommon in low-infected mosquitoes (≤5 oocysts, N = 80) where only two midguts had one intact oocyst.
evidence: Supported by microscopic examination data from 80 low-infected mosquitoes.

claim: 89% (33/37) of salivary gland sporozoite-positive mosquitoes in Burkina Faso expelled sporozoites.
source: Among 53 mosquitoes used for artificial skin feeding on day 16 PI, 89% (33/37) salivary gland sporozoite-positive mosquitoes with a median of 45,100 residual salivary gland sporozoites (IQR, 20,310–164,900) expelled a median of 1035 sporozoites (IQR, 171–2969).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 37 salivary gland sporozoite-positive mosquitoes.

claim: Salivary gland sporozoite-positive mosquitoes in Burkina Faso had a median of 45,100 residual salivary gland sporozoites (IQR 20,310–164,900).
source: Among 53 mosquitoes used for artificial skin feeding on day 16 PI, 89% (33/37) salivary gland sporozoite-positive mosquitoes with a median of 45,100 residual salivary gland sporozoites (IQR, 20,310–164,900) expelled a median of 1035 sporozoites (IQR, 171–2969).
evidence: Supported by qPCR quantification data from salivary gland sporozoite-positive mosquitoes.

claim: Mosquitoes in Burkina Faso expelled a median of 1035 sporozoites (IQR 171–2969).
source: Among 53 mosquitoes used for artificial skin feeding on day 16 PI, 89% (33/37) salivary gland sporozoite-positive mosquitoes with a median of 45,100 residual salivary gland sporozoites (IQR, 20,310–164,900) expelled a median of 1035 sporozoites (IQR, 171–2969).
evidence: Supported by qPCR quantification data from expelled sporozoites in artificial skin.

claim: The median number of salivary gland sporozoites per ruptured oocyst in An. coluzzii was 6350 (IQR 4225–8475).
source: We estimated a median of 6350 (IQR, 4225–8475) salivary gland sporozoites per ruptured oocyst in these experiments.
evidence: Estimated from experimental data analyzing the relationship between ruptured oocysts and salivary gland sporozoites in Burkina Faso experiments.

claim: Three skin samples in Burkina Faso were positive by COX-1 qPCR (range 1–64) while salivary glands were negative.
source: Three skin samples were positive by COX-1 qPCR (range 1–64) while salivary glands were negative, suggesting either all sporozoites were expelled or a technical failure in DNA extraction from the salivary glands.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from three mosquitoes with discordant results.

claim: Among 22 mosquitoes infected from three gametocyte donors in Burkina Faso, 10 unique P. falciparum clones were identified.
source: Among 22 mosquitoes that were infected from three gametocyte donors, we identified 10 unique clones
evidence: Supported by AMA-1 amplicon sequencing data from 22 mosquitoes.

claim: 68.2% (15/22) of infected mosquitoes tested in Burkina Faso harbored multiclonal infections.
source: 68.2% (15/22) of the infected mosquitoes that were tested harbored multiclonal infections.
evidence: Supported by AMA-1 amplicon sequencing data from 22 mosquitoes.

claim: 45.5% (10/22) of skin samples following probing contained more than one P. falciparum clone.
source: Following probing and successful sporozoite expelling, 10 skin samples contained more than one P. falciparum clone (45.5%; 10/22) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by AMA-1 amplicon sequencing data from 22 skin samples.

claim: 30% (16/53) of probing mosquitoes in Burkina Faso did not ingest blood.
source: During the artificial skin feeding, 30% (16/53) of probing mosquitoes did not ingest blood
evidence: Supported by observational data from 53 mosquitoes during artificial skin feeding.

claim: 68% (11/16) of mosquitoes that probed but did not ingest blood in Burkina Faso expelled sporozoites (range 1–11,970).
source: During the artificial skin feeding, 30% (16/53) of probing mosquitoes did not ingest blood, of which 68% (11/16) expelled sporozoites (range 1–11,970).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 16 mosquitoes that did not blood feed.

claim: There was a strong association between ruptured oocyst density and total salivary gland sporozoite density (ρ = 0.84, p<0.0001) in Burkina Faso experiments.
source: There was a strong association between ruptured oocyst density and total salivary gland sporozoite density (ρ = 0.84, 95% CI, 0.80–0.95; p<0.0001) (Figure 4C)
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis of experimental data from Burkina Faso.

claim: When intact oocysts were included in Burkina Faso analysis, the association between oocysts and salivary gland sporozoite density was very similar (ρ = 0.86, p<0.0001).
source: when intact oocysts were also included, the association was very similar (ρ = 0.86, p<0.0001; N = 30).
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis of experimental data from 30 mosquitoes.

claim: The correlation between oocyst density and salivary gland sporozoite density in Burkina Faso remained highly similar and statistically significant when examining different ranges of oocyst intensity (<5, <10, <20 oocysts).
source: When examining these associations for different ranges of oocyst intensity (<5, <10, <20 oocysts), correlation estimates remained highly similar and statistical significance was retained (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by stratified correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a strong positive association between total sporozoite load and the number of sporozoites expelled in Burkina Faso (ρ = 0.71, p<0.0001).
source: There was also a strong positive association between total sporozoite load and the number of sporozoites expelled (ρ = 0.71, 95% CI, 0.52–0.82; p<0.0001) (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis of experimental data from Burkina Faso.

claim: The correlation between total sporozoite load and expelling in Burkina Faso remained similar and statistically significant when examining different ranges of total sporozoite load (<10,000, <50,000, <100,000 sporozoites).
source: When examining this association between total sporozoite load and expelling for different ranges of total sporozoite load (<10,000, <50,000, <100,000 sporozoites), correlation estimates remained similar and statistically significant (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by stratified correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Approximately 95% of oocysts rupture to release sporozoites.
source: Through the visualization of ruptured oocysts and the simultaneous quantification of sporozoites that are expelled by individual mosquitoes, we observed that 95% of oocysts rupture to release sporozoites
evidence: Supported by experimental data from oocyst immunolabeling across experiments.

claim: Higher salivary gland sporozoite load is associated with shorter time to colonization of salivary glands.
source: Through the visualization of ruptured oocysts and the simultaneous quantification of sporozoites that are expelled by individual mosquitoes, we observed that 95% of oocysts rupture to release sporozoites and that higher salivary gland sporozoite load is associated with shorter time to colonization of salivary glands and larger inoculum size.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from EIP experiments showing earlier salivary gland positivity in highly infected mosquitoes.

claim: Higher salivary gland sporozoite load is associated with larger inoculum size.
source: Through the visualization of ruptured oocysts and the simultaneous quantification of sporozoites that are expelled by individual mosquitoes, we observed that 95% of oocysts rupture to release sporozoites and that higher salivary gland sporozoite load is associated with shorter time to colonization of salivary glands and larger inoculum size.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing positive correlation between total sporozoite load and expelled sporozoites.

claim: The entomological inoculation rate (EIR) is defined as the number of infectious bites per person per time unit and is the product of human biting rate and the proportion of sporozoite-positive mosquitoes.
source: The entomological inoculation rate (EIR) is defined as the number of infectious bites per person per time unit and is the product of human biting rate and the proportion of sporozoite-positive mosquitoes (Tusting et al., 2014; Shaukat et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to established definitions in the literature by Tusting et al., 2014 and Shaukat et al., 2010.

claim: EIR calculations assume all sporozoite-positive mosquitoes are equally infectious.
source: While EIR is a common measure of human malaria exposure, mosquito infection prevalence is used in this calculation and thus assumes all sporozoite-positive mosquitoes are equally infectious (Smith et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the description of EIR calculation methods and cited work by Smith et al., 2012.

claim: Assessments of the human infectious reservoir for malaria typically take the number of oocyst-positive mosquitoes as a measure of transmission and assume all oocysts will lead to salivary gland sporozoites and that all oocyst-positive mosquitoes have equal transmission potential.
source: Similarly, assessments of the human infectious reservoir for malaria typically take the number of oocyst-positive mosquitoes as a measure of transmission (Ouédraogo et al., 2016; Gonçalves et al., 2017) and thereby not only assume that all oocysts will lead to salivary gland sporozoites but also that all oocyst-positive mosquitoes have equal transmission potential.
evidence: Inferred from description of current assessment methods and cited works by Ouédraogo et al., 2016 and Gonçalves et al., 2017.

claim: Recent work with a rodent malaria model challenged the assumption that all oocyst-positive mosquitoes have equal transmission potential.
source: Recent work with a rodent malaria model challenged this central assumption (Aleshnick et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to work by Aleshnick et al., 2020.

claim: This study provides the first direct evidence for P. falciparum that sporozoite burden may be a relevant determinant in efficient sporozoite expelling.
source: we provide the first direct evidence for P. falciparum that sporozoite burden may indeed be a relevant determinant in efficient sporozoite expelling.
evidence: Based on the experimental findings showing associations between sporozoite burden and expelling.

claim: The estimate that ~95% of oocysts rupture is higher than a previous study with cultured gametocytes (~72%) that did not provide a second bloodmeal.
source: This estimate is higher than a previous study with cultured gametocytes (~72%) (Stone et al., 2013) that did not provide a second bloodmeal that may accelerate oocyst maturation (Shaw et al., 2020)
evidence: Comparison with cited previous work by Stone et al., 2013 and reference to Shaw et al., 2020 regarding second bloodmeal effects.

claim: A second bloodmeal may accelerate oocyst maturation.
source: This estimate is higher than a previous study with cultured gametocytes (~72%) (Stone et al., 2013) that did not provide a second bloodmeal that may accelerate oocyst maturation (Shaw et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to work by Shaw et al., 2020.

claim: A second bloodmeal better mimics natural feeding habits where multiple bloodmeals are taken within the period required for sporogony.
source: a second bloodmeal also better mimics natural feeding habits where multiple bloodmeals are taken within the period required for sporogony.
evidence: Based on knowledge of natural mosquito feeding behavior.

claim: Previous studies have shown that despite the substantial release of sporozoites per oocyst, only a proportion of sporozoites successfully reach the salivary glands.
source: Previous studies have shown that despite the substantial release of sporozoites per oocyst, only a proportion of sporozoites successfully reach the salivary glands (Rosenberg and Rungsiwongse, 1991; Hillyer et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by Rosenberg and Rungsiwongse, 1991 and Hillyer et al., 2007.

claim: The observed sporozoite estimates per oocyst (10,485–15,390) are higher than commonly reported.
source: Whilst these sporozoite estimates are higher than commonly reported (Graumans et al., 2020)
evidence: Comparison with cited review by Graumans et al., 2020.

claim: An early study from the 1960s reported microscopy-detected sporozoite densities above 9000 sporozoites per oocyst.
source: an early study from the 1960s reported microscopy-detected sporozoite densities above 9000 sporozoites per oocyst (Pringle, 1965)
evidence: Supported by citation to work by Pringle, 1965.

claim: A recent study using qPCR observed up to 12,583 sporozoites from a single oocyst.
source: a recent study using qPCR similarly observed up to 12,583 sporozoites from a single oocyst (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to work by Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Different from P. yoelii and P. berghei, only a minority of P. falciparum infected mosquitoes had sporozoite densities below threshold values previously reported in relation to a very low likelihood of achieving secondary infections.
source: These high sporozoite numbers per oocyst also mean that, different from P. yoelii (Aleshnick et al., 2020) and P. berghei (Churcher et al., 2017), only a minority of infected mosquitoes had sporozoite densities below the threshold values previously reported in relation to a very low likelihood of achieving secondary infections.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of experimental data with cited works by Aleshnick et al., 2020 and Churcher et al., 2017.

claim: Among infected An. stephensi mosquitoes with only one ruptured oocyst, 92.9% (26/28) had >1000 salivary gland sporozoites.
source: Even among infected An. stephensi mosquitoes with only one ruptured oocyst, 92.9% (26/28) had >1000 and 35.7% (10/28) had >10,000 sporozoites in their salivary glands.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 28 mosquitoes with single ruptured oocysts.

claim: Among infected An. stephensi mosquitoes with only one ruptured oocyst, 35.7% (10/28) had >10,000 sporozoites in their salivary glands.
source: Even among infected An. stephensi mosquitoes with only one ruptured oocyst, 92.9% (26/28) had >1000 and 35.7% (10/28) had >10,000 sporozoites in their salivary glands.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 28 mosquitoes with single ruptured oocysts.

claim: Only two mosquitoes with single oocysts were observed in Burkina Faso experiments and both had >10,000 salivary gland sporozoites.
source: In our experiments in natural gametocyte carriers in Burkina Faso, only two mosquitoes were observed with single oocysts and both had >10,000 salivary gland sporozoites.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Burkina Faso field experiments.

claim: 39% of sporozoite-positive mosquitoes across a wide range of infection densities failed to expel sporozoites upon probing.
source: Although P. falciparum sporozoite densities below these lower thresholds were thus uncommon, we observed that 39% of sporozoite-positive mosquitoes across a wide range of infection densities failed to expel sporozoites upon probing.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data showing that not all sporozoite-positive mosquitoes expelled sporozoites.

claim: An earlier study reported that 22% of P. yoelii-infected mosquitoes failed to expel sporozoites.
source: This finding broadly aligns with an earlier study of Medica and Sinnis that reported that 22% of P. yoelii-infected mosquitoes failed to expel sporozoites (Medica and Sinnis, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to work by Medica and Sinnis, 2005.

claim: For highly infected mosquitoes, inefficient expelling has been related to a decrease in apyrase in the mosquito saliva.
source: For highly infected mosquitoes, this inefficient expelling has been related to a decrease in apyrase in the mosquito saliva (Rossignol et al., 1984; Thiévent et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to works by Rossignol et al., 1984 and Thiévent et al., 2019.

claim: The association between salivary gland sporozoite density and expelled sporozoites was markedly stronger in An. coluzzii mosquitoes infected with natural gametocyte carriers compared to An. stephensi mosquitoes infected with cultured gametocytes.
source: Importantly, we observed a positive association between salivary gland sporozoite density and the number of expelled sporozoites. For unknown reasons, this association was markedly stronger in experiments where An. coluzzii mosquitoes were infected using blood from gametocyte carriers who were naturally infected with P. falciparum in Burkina Faso compared to An. stephensi mosquitoes infected with cultured gametocytes.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of correlation coefficients between the two experimental settings (ρ = 0.71 vs ρ = 0.35).

claim: In experiments with natural gametocyte carriers, sporozoite density appeared associated with both the likelihood of expelling any sporozoites and the inoculum size.
source: In our experiments with natural gametocyte carriers, sporozoite density appeared associated with both the likelihood of expelling any sporozoites and the inoculum size.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Burkina Faso showing trends in Figure 4B and correlation in Figure 4D.

claim: The most heavily infected mosquitoes expelled ~14-fold higher sporozoite numbers compared to the lowest quartile.
source: The most heavily infected mosquitoes expelled ~14-fold higher sporozoite numbers compared to the lowest quartile.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data comparing expelled sporozoites across infection intensity quartiles.

claim: Previous studies have not found consistent effects of parasite burden on EIP.
source: Previous studies have not found consistent effects of parasite burden on EIP (Guissou et al., 2023; Stopard et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to works by Guissou et al., 2023 and Stopard et al., 2021.

claim: Previous studies examining parasite burden effects on EIP were not specifically designed to examine this association across a broad range of infection intensities.
source: Previous studies have not found consistent effects of parasite burden on EIP (Guissou et al., 2023; Stopard et al., 2021) but, unlike our experiments, were also not specifically designed to examine this association across a broad range of infection intensities.
evidence: Comparison of study designs with cited previous works.

claim: Heavily infected mosquitoes may be infectious sooner and be more infectious.
source: Our associations of a shorter EIP in highly infected mosquitoes and, in separate experiments, a larger sporozoite inoculum size for highly infected mosquitoes make mosquito infection intensity a plausible factor in determining onward transmission potential to humans. Heavily infected mosquitoes may be infectious sooner and be more infectious.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing shorter EIP and larger inoculum in highly infected mosquitoes.

claim: Submicroscopic gametocyte carriers that typically result in low oocyst burdens in mosquitoes may give rise to infected mosquitoes with a reduced transmission potential.
source: On the other side of the infection spectrum, it is conceivable that submicroscopic gametocyte carriers that typically result in low oocyst burdens in mosquitoes give rise to infected mosquitoes with a reduced transmission potential.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the observed associations between infection burden and transmission metrics.

claim: If submicroscopic gametocyte carriers result in mosquitoes with reduced transmission potential, this would greatly reduce their importance for sustaining malaria transmission and make it less important to identify individuals with low parasite densities for malaria elimination purposes.
source: This would greatly reduce their importance for sustaining malaria transmission and make it less important to identify individuals with low parasite densities for malaria elimination purposes (Slater et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative inference about implications with citation to Slater et al., 2015.

claim: High sporozoite inocula were occasionally observed from mosquitoes with low infection intensity.
source: At the same time, we occasionally observed high sporozoite inocula from mosquitoes with low infection intensity.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in the data.

claim: The findings argue against a clear threshold sporozoite or oocyst density below which mosquitoes are truly irrelevant for transmission.
source: This argues against a clear threshold sporozoite or oocyst density below which mosquitoes are truly irrelevant for transmission.
evidence: Inferred from observations of sporozoite expelling from low-infected mosquitoes.

claim: The high number of sporozoites per oocyst makes it plausible that even low oocyst burdens (1–5 oocysts/infected gut) from asymptomatic parasite carriers would be sufficient to result in salivary gland sporozoite loads that can result in secondary infections.
source: Moreover, the high number of sporozoites per oocyst makes it plausible that even the low oocyst burdens that are typically observed from asymptomatic parasite carriers (in the range of 1–5 oocysts/infected gut; Andolina et al., 2021; Gonçalves et al., 2017) would be sufficient to result in salivary gland sporozoite loads that are sufficient to result in secondary infections.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on sporozoites per oocyst and cited typical oocyst burdens from Andolina et al., 2021 and Gonçalves et al., 2017.

claim: The infectivity of sporozoites at different time points post infection has been examined previously but never with individual mosquitoes.
source: Whilst the infectivity of sporozoites at different time points PI has been examined previously (Yang et al., 2017), these experiments have never been conducted with individual mosquitoes.
evidence: Comparison with cited previous work by Yang et al., 2017.

claim: The association between sporozoite inoculum size and the likelihood of achieving secondary infections may be best examined in controlled human infection studies.
source: Given striking differences in sporozoite burden between different Plasmodium species – low sporozoite densities appear considerably more common in mosquitoes infected with P. yoelii and P. berghei (Graumans et al., 2020; Churcher et al., 2017; Ahmed et al., 2021), and the inherent limitations of in vitro studies – the association between sporozoite inoculum size and the likelihood of achieving secondary infections may be best examined in controlled human infection studies.
evidence: Reasoned argument based on limitations of current approaches and cited differences between species from Graumans et al., 2020, Churcher et al., 2017, and Ahmed et al., 2021.

claim: Low sporozoite densities appear considerably more common in mosquitoes infected with P. yoelii and P. berghei compared to P. falciparum.
source: Given striking differences in sporozoite burden between different Plasmodium species – low sporozoite densities appear considerably more common in mosquitoes infected with P. yoelii and P. berghei (Graumans et al., 2020; Churcher et al., 2017; Ahmed et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to works by Graumans et al., 2020, Churcher et al., 2017, and Ahmed et al., 2021.

claim: CHMI experiments can be specifically designed to estimate the likelihood that probing by high- and low-infected mosquitoes results in blood-stage infection in malaria-naïve volunteers.
source: CHMI experiments can be specifically designed to estimate the likelihood that probing by (individual) high- and low-infected mosquitoes results in blood-stage infection in malaria-naïve volunteers.
evidence: Proposed experimental approach based on knowledge of CHMI methodology.

claim: CHMI studies are unique in allowing definitive evidence on the possible differences in infectiousness between high- and low-infected mosquitoes.
source: Whilst laborious, CHMI studies are unique in allowing definitive evidence on the possible differences in infectiousness between high- and low-infected mosquitoes.
evidence: Based on knowledge of CHMI study capabilities.

claim: The majority of oocysts rupture and contribute to salivary gland infection load.
source: In conclusion, we observed that the majority of oocysts rupture and contribute to salivary gland infection load.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing ~95% oocyst rupture rate.

claim: Salivary gland sporozoite load is highly variable.
source: We further observe that this sporozoite load is highly variable
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing wide ranges of sporozoite loads across mosquitoes.

claim: Salivary gland sporozoite load is an important determinant of the number of sporozoites that is expelled into the skin upon probing.
source: We further observe that this sporozoite load is highly variable and an important determinant of the number of sporozoites that is expelled into the skin upon probing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing positive correlations between sporozoite load and expelled sporozoites.

claim: P. falciparum gametocytes NF54 (West Africa) and NF135 (Cambodia) were cultured in an automated culture system.
source: P. falciparum gametocytes, NF54 (West Africa) and NF135 (Cambodia) (Conway et al., 2000; Teirlinck et al., 2013) were cultured in an automated culture system (Ponnudurai et al., 1982)
evidence: Supported by description of methods with citations to Conway et al., 2000, Teirlinck et al., 2013, and Ponnudurai et al., 1982.

claim: An. stephensi mosquitoes (Nijmegen Sind-Kasur strain) were reared at 30°C and 70–80% humidity with a 12 hr reverse day/night cycle.
source: An. stephensi mosquitoes, Nijmegen Sind-Kasur strain (Feldmann and Ponnudurai, 1989), were reared at 30°C and 70–80% humidity with a 12 hr reverse day/night cycle.
evidence: Supported by description of methods with citation to Feldmann and Ponnudurai, 1989.

claim: Gametocyte enrichment by MACS increased gametocyte concentration by approximately three- to fourfold.
source: Their blood was offered to locally reared Anopheles coluzzii via membrane feeders at the gametocyte density observed and following gametocyte enrichment by magnetic activated cell-sorting whereby gametocyte concentration was increased by approximately three- to fourfold.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from MACS enrichment procedures.

claim: Mosquitoes were given a second bloodmeal on days 4–6 post infection to synchronize oocyst development.
source: On days 4–6 PI, mosquitoes were given a second bloodmeal to synchronize oocyst development.
evidence: Supported by description of experimental methods.

claim: A previously published COX-1 primer set was modified to improve template annealing.
source: P. falciparum sporozoites were quantified by qPCR, targeting the mitochondrial gene COX-1. A previously published primer set (Boissière et al., 2013) was modified to improve template annealing
evidence: Supported by description of methods with citation to Boissière et al., 2013.
